title: Beijing attempts to trim overcapacity, but steers clear of structural issues
gist: MERICS's Overcapacity Monitor finds Chinese industry still produces more than domestic demand absorbs; Beijing's anti-'involution' campaign has worked in courier services (profits up nearly 10%) but struggles in EVs and solar, where stranded assets, easy entry and local-government incentives keep loss-making firms 'living badly, but not dying'. Europe should expect overcapacity to persist.

themes.theme: State of Chinese overcapacity (MERICS Overcapacity Monitor)

insights.claim: China's industry continues to produce more than domestic demand can absorb, generating excess capacity across various industries that is putting pressure on global markets.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Export-driven deflationary pressure on global manufactured-goods prices persists; competitors in Europe should expect continued price pressure.

themes.theme: Why involution persists: state support and local incentives

insights.claim: Since 2025 Beijing has campaigned against 'involution' — large-scale cutthroat competition for market share that produces chronically low profits or losses and is a primary symptom of overcapacity in key industries.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Anti-involution policy is the main lever to watch for any change in Chinese pricing behaviour.
insights.locator: China’s government continues efforts to fight

insights.claim: Unlike a normal business cycle where weaker firms are displaced and consolidation restores equilibrium, Chinese government support lets firms sustain razor-thin margins and losses for extended periods, delaying consolidation.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Normal cyclical bottoming signals (bankruptcies, consolidation) arrive much later in China, prolonging global price pressure.
insights.quote: in China, government support helps companies sustain razor-thin margins and even losses for extended periods, delaying consolidation

insights.claim: Citing the OECD, Chinese firms received on average three to eight times more government support than OECD-based firms, a conservative estimate; subsidies, cheap financing and municipal protectionism keep weak firms alive.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Scale of subsidy gap underpins trade-defence arguments (anti-subsidy duties) in Europe and elsewhere.

insights.claim: Loss-making firms propped up by public support drain public resources: they leave few funds for R&D, erode tax intake and raise debt; the IMF estimates China's debt could reach 127% of GDP by 2031, up from 99.2% in 2025.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Overcapacity is a fiscal problem too — rising public debt constrains Beijing's future stimulus capacity.
insights.quote: The IMF has estimated debt could reach 127 percent of GDP by 2031 (up from 99.2 percent in 2025)

insights.claim: Local officials have reasons to tolerate involution: their career performance indicators reward steady employment, sunk-cost dynamics make it politically hard to let failing projects die, and firms and officials bet on a breakthrough or outlasting rivals.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Bottom-up political incentives structurally resist capacity cuts, limiting the effectiveness of top-down campaigns.

insights.claim: The result is many Chinese firms 'living badly, but not dying' — zombie-like persistence rather than exit.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Expect prolonged low-margin zombie competition rather than a sharp shakeout.

themes.theme: Courier services: the anti-involution success case

insights.claim: The most successful anti-involution case has been courier services, where from 2025 regulators and major players established and raised price floors; by September 2026 profits had risen nearly ten percent in major markets, with similar trends in food delivery and e-commerce.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Price-floor coordination works in asset-light, price-competed sectors — supportive for Chinese logistics/platform margins.

themes.theme: EV sector: stranded assets make involution hard to manage

insights.claim: Methods that worked for couriers don't transfer to EVs: gig-economy supply scales up and down easily, while EV production requires vast asset investment with sunk-cost and stranded-asset risk if factories close, worsened by years of local-government industrial policy.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: EV overcapacity is likely to be among the most persistent, keeping pressure on global auto pricing and exports.

insights.claim: Price floors are unlikely to work for EVs because quality and price vary widely; the lowest-quality makers must offer rock-bottom prices and consumers are unlikely to pay more under a floor.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Don't expect a courier-style margin recovery for low-end Chinese EV makers; consolidation, not pricing pacts, is needed.
insights.quote: It is unlikely that consumers would pay higher prices resulting from a price floor.

themes.theme: Wind vs solar: consolidation determines policy effectiveness

insights.claim: China's wind turbine sector has consolidated from nearly 80 producers in 2010 to 10 in 2025, because turbines are design-intensive and less commoditized, preventing rapid entry and capacity expansion.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: A consolidated wind industry has pricing discipline; less exposed to involution-driven losses than solar.

insights.claim: In 2025 China could have met global demand for solar PV while leaving 40 percent of its production capacity idle.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Massive solar overhang implies continued global module price pressure and margin distress for producers.
insights.quote: In 2025, China could have met global demand for solar PVs while leaving 40 percent of its production capacity idle.

insights.claim: Fewer players allowed the wind sector a 2024 self-discipline pact not to price below cost, plus demand-side benchmark pricing in turbine tenders; solar's easy entry (readily available machinery and inputs) and commoditization have blocked comparable capacity cuts or price floors.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Market structure predicts whether anti-involution coordination succeeds — a useful screen for which Chinese sectors may see margin repair.

insights.claim: As a result, solar involution has produced far steeper price declines and loss-making among firms, whereas wind prices dropped and margins were squeezed but not into losses.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Solar remains the more distressed sector; wind manufacturers have more resilient profitability.

insights.claim: European policymakers and corporate strategists should continue to expect overcapacity and involution in many sectors and should not take Beijing's pledges as indicative of success.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: European industry should plan for sustained Chinese price competition and lean on trade defence rather than Chinese self-correction.
